interviewQuestions.question: Explain PCA to someone non-technical
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain PCA to someone non-technical?**

I'd open with an analogy before any math: imagine photographing a pancake. Shot from directly above, you barely see its thickness — but you don't need to, because almost nothing interesting happens along that axis. Shot from the side, you'd capture the thickness but lose the shape that actually matters.

PCA does the equivalent for data with hundreds of measurements per item: it finds the "best camera angle" — the handful of directions along which the data actually varies the most — and lets you drop the rest without losing much of the story. For example, a retailer with 50 correlated customer metrics (spend, visits, returns, etc.) might compress them into 3-4 components that still capture 90% of what distinguishes customers, making the data faster to analyze and plot.

**Testing:** whether you can translate a linear-algebra technique into a mental model a non-technical stakeholder would actually retain, without leaning on the word 'eigenvector.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Explaining PCA in plain language

interviewQuestions.question: When would you deliberately not use PCA before modeling?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
⭐ **Q: When would you deliberately not use PCA before modeling?**

My first flag: whenever the business needs to explain *which original feature* drove a prediction. PCA's components are linear blends of the originals, so once you've transformed the data, you can no longer point to "customer tenure" as the driver — you're pointing at an opaque mix. Regulated domains like credit or healthcare, where a decision has to be explainable, are the clearest example.

I'd also skip it when the relationships in the data are strongly non-linear — PCA only finds linear directions of variance, so it can flatten away exactly the structure a tree-based model or a non-linear method like UMAP would have used. And for small feature counts (say under 10-15), the compression usually isn't worth the interpretability cost at all.

**Testing:** whether you understand PCA's real cost (loss of interpretability, linear-only structure) rather than reciting it as a default preprocessing step for everything.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Knowing when to skip PCA
